articles.headline: OFAC Announces Settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, International Criminal Court Designation, and Burma Sanctions Removal
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics. This action was part of a broader set of updates from OFAC.

Concurrently, OFAC issued a designation related to the International Criminal Court (ICC) and accompanying General Licenses. This move follows a trend of targeted sanctions and the provision of specific authorizations to mitigate unintended consequences.

Additionally, OFAC announced a Burma-related designation removal, indicating a recalibration of sanctions policy concerning Myanmar. These actions reflect ongoing adjustments to U.S. sanctions programs globally.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued a new General License pertaining to Russia. This license provides specific authorizations for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under the Russia-related sanctions program.

The issuance of new General Licenses is a common practice by OFAC to clarify the scope of sanctions and to allow for activities deemed permissible or necessary. Details of the authorized transactions are available in the full text of the license.
This action comes as part of OFAC's ongoing management of the extensive sanctions regime against Russia, which has seen continuous adjustments and clarifications since its inception.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities, Issues New GL, and Amends Russia-Related GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations, targeting entities and individuals involved in activities deemed sanctionable under U.S. policy. These designations aim to further pressure the Iranian regime.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC also issued a new Iran-related General License, providing specific authorizations for certain transactions. This often accompanies new sanctions to ensure humanitarian aid or other permissible activities can continue.

Furthermore, OFAC issued an amended Russia-related General License, indicating adjustments to existing authorizations concerning Russia. These concurrent actions highlight the dynamic nature of U.S. sanctions policy across multiple geopolitical fronts.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Designations Removals, Updates, and Iran-Related Guidance
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced several designations removals and updates, indicating a review and adjustment of its sanctions lists. These changes can reflect shifts in policy or the cessation of sanctionable activities by listed parties.

Additionally, OFAC published an Iran-related OFAC Alert and an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). This guidance aims to provide clarity to the public and financial institutions regarding compliance with Iran sanctions.
The publication of alerts and amended FAQs is a regular practice by OFAC to help stakeholders understand and adhere to complex sanctions regulations, particularly in evolving geopolitical landscapes.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Terrorism Designations, targeting individuals and entities involved in supporting terrorist activities. These designations aim to disrupt financial networks and limit the operational capabilities of terrorist organizations.

These actions fall under OFAC's broader mandate to combat global terrorism financing through economic sanctions. The designations typically result in the blocking of assets and prohibition of transactions with the designated parties.
The U.S. government continues to utilize its sanctions authorities to address threats to national security posed by international terrorism.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities and Transnational Criminal Organizations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and designations updates, targeting entities and individuals connected to the Iranian regime. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to exert economic pressure on Iran.

Additionally, OFAC designated a Transnational Criminal Organization (TCO), aiming to disrupt illicit financial activities and criminal networks operating across borders. This highlights OFAC's dual focus on state-sponsored and criminal threats.
The announcement also included the publication of an Iran-related Determination and an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question, providing further clarity and legal basis for the new measures.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Terrorism and Transnational Criminal Organization Designations, Removes Belarus, Narcotics, and Libya Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting Counter Terrorism and Transnational Criminal Organizations, reinforcing its commitment to disrupting illicit networks globally. These actions aim to sever financial ties and limit the operational reach of these groups.

In a separate but concurrent action, OFAC also announced the removal of designations related to Belarus, Counter Narcotics, and Libya. These removals suggest a re-evaluation of specific sanctions targets or a response to changed circumstances in these regions.
This dual approach of new designations and removals demonstrates OFAC's dynamic strategy in managing its sanctions programs, adapting to evolving threats and geopolitical shifts.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Counter Narcotics, Counter Terrorism, Iran-Related, and Non-Proliferation Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a broad set of new designations, targeting individuals and entities across multiple sanctions programs. These include Counter Narcotics, Counter Terrorism, Iran-related, and Non-Proliferation designations.

This comprehensive action underscores the U.S. government's commitment to addressing a wide array of national security threats through economic sanctions. The designations aim to disrupt illicit activities and financial networks supporting these malign actors.

The simultaneous application of sanctions across diverse categories highlights a coordinated effort to maximize pressure on those engaged in drug trafficking, terrorism, proliferation, and activities supporting the Iranian regime.

articles.headline: OFAC Publishes Regulatory Amendments, New Cuba Sanctions Regulations, and Related Guidance
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the publication of significant regulatory amendments, including new Cuba Sanctions Regulations. These updates reflect a recalibration of U.S. policy towards Cuba.

The new regulations implement Executive Order 14404 of May 1, 2026, which focuses on imposing sanctions on those responsible for repression in Cuba and threats to U.S. national security and foreign policy.

Accompanying these regulatory changes, OFAC also issued new and amended Cuba-related Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) and a Cuba-related OFAC Alert to provide guidance and clarify compliance obligations for the public.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Venezuela General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the issuance of amended Venezuela General Licenses. These amendments modify existing authorizations for certain transactions related to Venezuela, reflecting ongoing adjustments to U.S. sanctions policy.

General Licenses are crucial tools used by OFAC to provide specific permissions for activities that would otherwise be prohibited under a sanctions program. The amendments often clarify scope, extend deadlines, or introduce new conditions.
Companies operating under Venezuela authorizations are advised to confirm they are relying on the current version of each license to ensure compliance with the updated regulations.

articles.headline: OCC Assesses $350 Million Penalty Against American Express National Bank for BSA/AML Failures
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced a cease-and-desist order and a $350 million civil money penalty against American Express National Bank for significant deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and anti-money laundering (AML) compliance program.

The OCC found that the bank failed to establish and maintain a BSA/AML compliance program reasonably designed to assure and monitor compliance with regulations. Deficiencies included inadequate resources, insufficient staff expertise, systemic internal control gaps, weak independent testing, and inadequate BSA/AML training.

Crucially, the bank failed to tailor its BSA/AML risk assessment to its business activities, focusing too narrowly on demand deposit accounts and insufficiently on its more dominant credit and charge card products. This resulted in a failure to timely identify and report approximately $13 billion of suspected trade-based money laundering activity over the past decade.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency / Traders Union

articles.headline: BIS Eases Export Controls for UAE, Upgrades Status
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced a significant upgrade to the status of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR).

This deregulatory action recognizes the UAE's status as a U.S. Major Defense Partner and its support in advancing U.S. national security interests. As a result, the UAE will be removed from EAR Country Groups D:3 and D:4.
The change will eliminate restrictions on support for the UAE's unmanned aerial vehicle programs and generally enhance favorable treatment for the country under U.S. export controls.

articles.headline: BIS to Control Export of Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors
body: Effective November 20, 2026, the export of certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors will be subject to the Bureau of Industry and Security's (BIS) Export Administration Regulations (EAR), rather than the State Department's U.S. Munitions List.

This deregulatory action aims to align export controls on suppressors with those already applied to firearms, alleviating compliance burdens on the firearms industry while continuing to protect national security.

Under this new rule, suppressors will be added to the Commerce Control List (CCL), and BIS will require a license for certain exports, reexports, or in-country transfers, including releases of related software and technology to foreign persons. License exceptions available for firearms will also apply to suppressors.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.

articles.headline: Meet India's feisty Gen Z protester who is taking on Modi
body: Neha Bora has emerged as one of the most recognisable faces from India's recent Gen Z-led protests.

articles.headline: BBC breaks down video of the aftermath of New York City ICE shooting
body: The BBC's Nada Tawfik goes through new dramatic body cam footage that shows the tense moments when police arrive on scene.

articles.headline: How the trial of murdered Australian brothers and US friend unfolded
body: The mother of two Australian surfers murdered in Mexico two years ago with their American friend said "accountability matters".
